name: Sunbed + MT2 stack

lead: The stack combines melanotan II, an unlicensed tanning peptide, with tanning bed sessions to darken skin faster. It circulates in looksmaxxing tanning discussions.
No studies were found testing the combination.

paras: Melanotan II mimics alpha-MSH to stimulate melanin production, while UV light triggers tanning directly. Proponents expect the two to add together; this has not been studied.

Melanotan II is unlicensed and regulators warn against it. UV tanning devices are classified as carcinogenic and linked to higher melanoma risk; reviews note melanoma reports in melanotan users may reflect extra UV exposure.

lead: The sunbed plus MT2 stack is a looksmaxxing practice of combining indoor tanning sessions with melanotan II (MT2), an unlicensed alpha-MSH analogue, with the stated goal of building pigment faster than either alone [1][2].

Melanotan II was never approved as a medicine, and health agencies have warned against unlicensed use since 2007 [1]. UV exposure from tanning devices is classified by the WHO's IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen [2]. Reviews of melanoma in melanotan users have said reported increases could probably be explained by heavier UV exposure [1]. No clinical trial of the combination was found.
infobox: Not licensed anywhere as a medicine [1]

paras: Practitioners pair melanotan with UV exposure because melanotan peptides are thought to stimulate melanocytes, while UV provides the signal that drives tanning. The pairing is discussed as a way to shorten the time to visible pigment. This article does not describe dosing or procedures.

Melanotan II was developed in the 1980s at the University of Arizona as a possible sunless tanning agent, and Palatin ceased developing it in 2000 [1]. Products sold online are unlicensed; agencies in the UK, Norway, Denmark, Ireland and the US have warned about legality, safety case reports and impurities [1]. Reported effects include flushing, nausea and darkening of moles [1].

Tanning beds were introduced commercially in the late 1970s [2]. IARC's 2009 review classified UV radiation as carcinogenic to humans; a 2014 meta-analysis found 16% higher melanoma risk among indoor tanners, 35% when use began before age 25 [2]. The FDA requires a warning against use by under-18s on devices [2].

No studies found on combining melanotan with sunbed use. Reviews of melanotan II alone found no conclusive evidence of melanoma causation in 2013, and a 2021 review said excess melanoma in users could probably be explained by more UV exposure [1].

timeline.event: Health agencies begin warning against unlicensed melanotan. [1]
IARC classifies UV tanning devices as carcinogenic to humans. [2]
